data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided it is framed strictly as a methodological rule based on the asymmetry of risk rather than a prediction of future success.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly stated that choosing the better-corroborated theory implies a belief in its higher probability of being true in the future.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the defense requires attributing any predictive power or pragmatic advantage to corroboration beyond the immediate avoidance of known falsification.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If it can be demonstrated that the 'asymmetry of risk' argument implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature (induction) to hold valid for the next test.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven) and the pragmatic decision of which theory to act upon. The mechanism relies on the 'asymmetry of risk': acting on a falsified or poorly tested theory carries a known high risk of failure, whereas acting on a severely tested (corroborated) theory, while offering no guarantee of truth, avoids the known error. This choice is a rational wager on the current state of critical discussion, not an inductive inference that the future will resemble the past.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
